claims.text: The starting material is a crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle containing at least five metals.
Tungsten and molybdenum are refractory metals.
A minor amount of tungsten or molybdenum can be incorporated into the specified solid-solution nanoparticles.
Introducing a minor amount of tungsten or molybdenum can overcome structural or chemical instability during operation at 773–1173 K.
The added refractory-metal atoms reduce diffusion rates in the nanoparticles.
The added refractory-metal atoms suppress defect formation in the nanoparticles.
Reduced diffusion and suppressed defect formation preserve nanoparticle structural stability.
Reduced diffusion and suppressed defect formation preserve nanoparticle chemical stability.
Refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles will be more stable than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the addition.
Refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the addition.
The proposed operating window is 773–1173 K for periods ranging from hours to days.
X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy can be used to monitor the thermal-exposure test.
Structural changes, chemical changes, catalytic activity, and catalytic selectivity are the proposed experimental response variables.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified nanoparticles show significant structural or chemical instability, or fail to improve catalytic performance relative to the unmodified control.
